way-in.heading: That bridge is
way-in.text:
The road turns to dirt and carves through the forest until it runs out. You park, and from there you walk, under a canopy that closes over the trail behind you.

Around the last curve the laurel opens up, and there it is: a hundred feet of suspended bridge strung with small warm lights, swaying over the holler, with a creek running somewhere below. A thirty-foot bridge before it is the warm-up. At the far end, at the top of the last stair, the door handle is oak, burnished by the hands of every guest who came before you.

That bridge is the front door.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:25-29 (the Writer's "The way in"; its "Ten minutes" left out: a time in minutes with no fact row)
way-in.alt: The rope bridge at night, strung with warm lights

treehouse.heading: A canvas peak,
treehouse.text:
At dusk the canvas peak glows from the inside, like a lantern somebody lit for you. The treehouse is hand-built, sixty feet up, on forty-two acres of forest in Dahlonega, Georgia.

The windows work like a tent's: canvas you roll up and tie back. A chandelier hangs over the bed, on a dimmer. Out on the deck there's a fire table. Up on the Sky Deck there's a pizza oven, and a cast iron pan that goes into it and cooks just about anything, from eggs to steak. There's a projector screen for movie night. The water comes from the property's own well.

There is no stove and no fridge. There's a big cooler on the deck, and you bring the ice.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:31-35 (the Writer's "The treehouse", canon only; its "Downtown Dahlonega is about ten minutes away" left out: minutes with no fact row)
treehouse.alt: The bed beneath the treehouse windows

bridge.heading: One hundred feet
bridge.text:
A hundred feet long. Sixty feet up. It hangs between two white oaks over the holler, strung with small warm lights that come on at dark and burn for two or three hours. The planks are white oak, salvaged and milled from standing dead trees on this land. A crew of riggers from North Carolina strung its first cables.

It sways. That's by design. The ropes are chest-high and the planks are solid. It's rated for eight people at one time, everyone counted, and that number is the engineer's, not ours.

Every guest crosses it. It isn't optional. It's the way home. For a wedding it's the aisle.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:37-41 (the Writer's "The bridge"; "or the altar" left out: words Mick has not heard)
bridge.alt: From above: the hundred-foot rope bridge through the canopy at golden hour

mornings.heading: Nowhere
mornings.text:
Every morning, around 8:30, fresh pastries wait in the TreeMail box where you enter the bridges.

Or take the Dawn Table. Breakfast made from scratch and carried by hand across the bridge to your door. There is always more than you can finish, and there is always premium champagne with fresh-squeezed orange juice.

Eat it on the deck while the light comes up. The mist lifts off the valley. The first birds call. The leaves above you glow gold, then green, then gold again, and there's nowhere you have to be.
sources: loxley-rescue/canon/voice.md:58 (made from scratch, carried by hand)
mornings.alt: Morning sun flaring through the canopy, the treehouse small among the trees

who-we-are.heading: Built by the family
who-we-are.text:
We're Mick and Livy. We found this land on a cold January morning, with fog still burning off the valley, down a driveway lined with mountain laurel. Two hundred feet in, before we'd even seen the house, Livy said, “This is it. Come on.”

Mick saw the engineering. Livy saw the experience. Every beam was carried four hundred feet down the mountain by hand, because we loved the forest too much to bring in machines. Mick built much of the framing himself. Livy insisted on a full bathroom sixty feet up, because she wasn't climbing down a tree in the middle of the night, and neither should anyone else.

We live here, with two little girls who think rope bridges are a normal way to get home. Book direct and you deal with the family who built it.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:49-53 (the Writer's "Who we are", Our Story's own words)
who-we-are.alt: The steel and wood frame beneath the treehouse, in fall colour

how-it-works.heading: Tell us the day.
how-it-works.text:
Write to us with the day you have in mind and what it's for. We answer fast. If you'd rather talk, call or text 706-502-4823.

For a stay, the calendar does the rest. Choose your dates and the total appears, taxes and cleaning included, with your booking agreement shown in full before you pay.

For a ceremony, we talk it through first. Then we send the agreement. It is shorter than it looks, and we settle the ceremony time together closer to the day. Sign it, and the date is yours.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:55-59 (the Writer's "How it works"; "Every open night shows its rate" and "the whole price appears" replaced by the site's own "the total appears": the price guard)

form-intro.text: Tell us the day you have in mind. A date, or just a month. How many of you. What it's for, in your own words. We answer fast.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:61-62 (the Writer's form intro; the per-set second lines, with their slots, left out)

dahlonega-found.heading: A small town with wineries
dahlonega-found.text:
There's a place in the North Georgia foothills where the road drops through a tunnel of mountain laurel so thick the branches nearly meet overhead.

Some of Livy's friends had been to a wedding in a small town with wineries and mountains, a place called Dahlonega. “What about there?” she said. Mick had never heard of it. Dahlonega was supposed to be a weekend away, not a life change.

So on a cold January morning, with fog still burning off the valley, they drove down a driveway lined with mountain laurel. Livy said it before they had even seen the house: “This is it. Come on.”

They live here now: Mick, Livy, Aurora and Tilly Mac. When you arrive, the people who designed and built your treehouse are the same people handing you a welcome basket.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/our_story.py:35 ("just over an hour from Atlanta" left out here)
dahlonega-found.alt: Fog lifting through tall hardwoods, morning light coming through the trunks

dahlonega-aisle.heading: The bridge becomes the aisle.
dahlonega-aisle.text:
Your ceremony begins on solid ground. You walk together toward the rope bridge: a hundred feet of suspended pathway over the forest floor, swaying gently between two ancient white oaks. Every step is a choice. Every step is toward each other. By the time you reach the other side, the ordinary world is behind you, and you're standing in the canopy, sixty feet above the earth.

Say your vows on the deck of a treehouse a family built with their own hands. Let the forest witness it. Let the silence hold it.

Then stay the night. Wake up married in the sky.
dahlonega-aisle.alt: The rope bridge running through fall leaves to the treehouse canvas

dahlonega-town.heading: Gold rush history
dahlonega-town.text:
Dahlonega sits at the heart of Georgia's wine country. The square still has its courthouse with the gold-leaf steeple, surrounded by local shops, restaurants and places that have nothing to do with a chain.

Picnic Cafe is small-town, personal, genuine: great sandwiches and baked goods, the perfect quick lunch before you explore the square. Everyone stops at the Dahlonega Fudge Factory, family-owned since 1982. It's part of the trip. Paul Thomas Chocolates makes more than 120 handmade recipes on site, for couples who want something special to bring back to the treehouse.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/local_guide.py:54-55 (its 1828 date left to the fact rows, which cite the city)

law-license.heading: From a Georgia
law-license.text:
The statute says marriage licenses “shall be issued only by the judge of the probate court or his clerk” (O.C.G.A. § 19-3-30(a)).

The statute says that if neither of you is a Georgia resident, “the license shall be issued in the county in which the ceremony is to be performed” (§ 19-3-30(b)(2)). Loxley Forest is in Lumpkin County.

The statute says that if one of you is a Georgia resident, “the license may be issued in any county of this state” (§ 19-3-30(b)(2)).

The statute says a license “may be issued immediately and without any waiting period” (§ 19-3-35).

The statute says the application is “verified by oath of the applicants” (§ 19-3-33(a)), and “The judge shall require all applicants to furnish the court with documentary evidence of proof of age” (§ 19-3-36). Ask the court what else to bring.

law-asks.heading: No waiting period,
law-asks.text:
Georgia's probate judges' council says: “As of July 1, 2003, premarital blood tests are no longer required.” The Code's note to § 19-3-40 carries the repeal.

What a license costs, with and without a premarital course, is on the court's page, linked below, read [date].

The statute says each of you must “be at least 18 years of age” (§ 19-3-2(a)(2)), and it sets separate conditions for an applicant who is 17 (§ 19-3-2(b)); ask the court.

The statute says the application form lets each of you designate “the surnames which will be used as their legal surnames after the marriage is consummated” (§ 19-3-33.1(a)).

The Supreme Court says: “The Court, in this decision, holds same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry in all States.” (Obergefell v. Hodges, 576 U.S. 644 (2015)).
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-counsel-elope-in-georgia.md:28 (P7, the Critic's fix: the cost is the court's page's; [date] waits for the live read)

law-officiant.heading: Your officiant,
law-officiant.text:
The statute says the license is directed to officials it names, among them judges and magistrates, and to a “minister, or other person of any religious society or sect authorized by the rules of such society to perform the marriage ceremony” (§ 19-3-30(c)). We arrange your officiant.

The statute says your officiant must “return the license to the judge of the probate court ... within 30 days after the date of the marriage” (§ 19-3-30(c)), and that after it is recorded the judge “shall return to the parties to a marriage the license” (§ 19-3-44(a)).
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-counsel-elope-in-georgia.md:35 (P14: "We arrange your officiant." beside it, the held card, log:3036)

law-house.heading: Your license
law-house.text:
Your license is yours: we do not handle licenses and cannot get one for you.

This page quotes Georgia's code and the Lumpkin County Probate Court's own page, read on [date]. It is general information, not legal advice. For your own situation, ask the court or a lawyer.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-counsel-elope-in-georgia.md:36 (P15; [date] waits for the court's page read live)

cost-shape.heading: What an elopement
cost-shape.text:
An elopement in Georgia asks for four things, and only the first is the law's.

The license. It comes from a Georgia probate court, and the court's own page says what it costs.

An officiant. Yours is arranged by us, and is an independent contractor, not our employee.

Photographs. Bring your own photographer if you like; anyone you bring to work is your guest and follows our safety rules.

The nights. Every package begins with a two-night treehouse stay, sixty feet up.

What our packages come to, we send by reply. Write to us with the day you have in mind, and the answer carries every number.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-counsel-elope-in-georgia.md:28 (P7: the cost is the court's page's)
new words: the framing, and "we send by reply" (no price on the site without Mick's yes)
cost-shape.alt: The rope bridge stretching through the trees toward the treehouse in fall

cost-packages.heading: Three tiers.
cost-packages.text:
The Vow holds a two-night treehouse stay, your choice of ceremony site, the Fire Circle or the treehouse deck, a vetted officiant, a seasonal bouquet and boutonniere, a champagne toast, and romantic room preparation.

The Crossing holds everything in The Vow, plus the rope bridge ceremony, the Builder's Tour with Mick, golden hour timing, photography coordination, a curated dinner, The Morning After, and a celebration cake.

The Elevation adds to The Crossing a floral ceremony arch, a premium welcome hamper, a celebration brunch, full day-of coordination, and photography timed to the day's best moments.

Every Loxley elopement is personally coordinated. No two ceremonies are the same.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/elopements.py:26-50 (the packages as the live page lists them; The Elevation's "Private chef dinner" not repeated: a banned phrase)

december.heading: Frost on
december.text:
Some mornings there's frost on the rope bridge. The canopy is stripped to its bones, and it shows views you can't see the rest of the year. The fire pit feels essential. Down in town, Old Fashioned Christmas turns Dahlonega into the Christmas Town of the Southeast.

Back up the trail the silence is deeper and the stars are brighter. The treehouse is heated, and nights run to about 32 degrees in December at the nearest station with records, in Helen. Sunset comes early, around 5:27 pm in mid December, and the bridge lights come on to meet you.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:114-116 (the Writer's December block; "December is Frost Season." left out: the month-to-season mapping Mick has not heard)
december.alt: The treehouse canvas glowing at night beside the lit rope bridge

christmas-sky.heading: The sky
christmas-sky.text:
When the leaves drop and the canopy opens, November through early spring, the night sky from your deck is staggering. No light pollution. The Milky Way isn't something you look up at. It's something you're inside.

The fire table on the sky deck keeps you out there longer.

christmas-fire.heading: The Fire Circle
christmas-fire.text:
The Fire Circle is a boulder fire pit that looks like it emerged from the earth centuries ago, set at the four compass points. It echoes traditions that have existed for thousands of years. We light the fire and tend it ourselves.

Exchange rings beside it, or say your vows out on the bridge, where it becomes the aisle.

Flower petals, bubbles, and battery candles are very welcome.
sources: loxley-rescue/canon/agreements/elopement-hosting.md:51 (we light and tend the fire; petals, bubbles, battery candles)
christmas-fire.alt: The stone fire pit on the forest floor, ringed with ferns

atlanta-drive.heading: Just over an hour
atlanta-drive.text:
We're in the foothills above Dahlonega, just over an hour north of Atlanta. Detailed directions come with your booking confirmation.

Most people don't have two or three weeks to paddle into the wilderness and set up camp. They have a weekend. Maybe two nights between the obligations that never stop pulling at them. They want the silence, the forest and the feeling of being truly away, without the time, the gear or the trail miles to earn it the hard way.

That's what Loxley was designed to solve. Not a hotel room with a view. A night in the forest that changes how you feel when you drive home on Sunday.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:196-199 (the Writer's frame D: "about 70 minutes by car, traffic allowing" left out, minutes with no fact row; "The last mile is a mountain road" left out, a distance in miles)
atlanta-drive.alt: The sun low over a ridge of fall trees under a clear sky

atlanta-without.heading: No ballrooms.
atlanta-without.text:
No ballrooms. No banquet chairs. No receiving line. Just two people, an ancient forest, and a ceremony as dramatic as the love that brought you here.

Loxley Forest is a private home on forty-two private acres, and you are coming as our overnight guests. Your ceremony is an experience we host as part of your stay.

Say your vows on the bridge, beside the Fire Circle on the forest floor, or on the private deck of your treehouse, sixty feet in the air.

vow-renewal.heading: Say them again
vow-renewal.heading_em: with no one but the trees
vow-renewal.text:
You said them once in front of everyone. Say them again with no one but the trees.

Pick the place. Out on the bridge, a hundred feet long and sixty feet up, with the holler under you. On the deck, in the canopy, level with the hawks. Or beside the Fire Circle, the boulder fire pit on the forest floor, with the fire going. Say the old words, or the ones you know now.

Tell us what you're celebrating when you write, and we'll make it right.

Afterward the night is yours: dinner by the fire, the bridge lights small and warm behind you, and a bed sixty feet up.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:170-175 (the Writer's vow renewal block: new words; the officiant and the places for a renewal are Mick's call)
vow-renewal.alt: The treehouse deck with chairs, above the forest

renewal-crossing.heading: Your heart
renewal-crossing.text:
The thirty-foot bridge is the warm-up. Next come your first steps across the hundred-footer. The ground drops away. The trees rise to meet you. Your hands grip the ropes and your heart beats faster. Halfway across, you stop noticing the height and start noticing the silence.

Sit with the person you love and hear nothing but the creek and the wind in the canopy.
renewal-crossing.alt: The start of the rope bridge in fall

renewal-built.heading: Built,
renewal-built.text:
The treehouse is a tetrahedron frame, steel sandwiched between wood, suspended from living oaks by specialized hardware. Every piece was carried down four hundred feet of mountain without a single machine touching the forest. It took nine months, three times longer than planned.

The deck planks are white oak, salvaged and milled from standing dead trees on the property. Wood that was already here, given a second life.

How many people can say they've spent the night hanging from five oak trees, sixty feet in the air, with nothing between them and the stars but canvas and canopy?

That's the rhythm of Loxley Forest. Build. Pause for the family. Build again.
renewal-built.alt: The treehouse platform seen from the forest floor, its wooden truss overhead

renewal-fire.heading: A dinner you cooked yourself
renewal-fire.text:
Build your own fire in the eight-foot pit on the forest floor and cook over the open flame. The fire pit grill hammers into the pit. There is a skillet for steak and eggs.

Steaks, burgers, foil packets, whatever you bring. There's something primal about a dinner you cooked yourself under the stars.
sources: loxley-rescue/canon/voice.md:126 (the grill over the Fire Circle)

courthouse-same.heading: One license,
courthouse-same.text:
Both begin the same way: a marriage license from a Georgia probate court, which is yours to get. We do not handle licenses and cannot get one for you.

A courthouse wedding is that license and an official to say the words over it. The statute names the officials who may, among them judges and magistrates (§ 19-3-30(c)).

An elopement is the same license and the same vows, with a day built around them. Here that day has a hundred-foot rope bridge for an aisle, a fire on the forest floor, and a treehouse sixty feet up to wake in.

Either way, the license goes back to the court: the statute says your officiant must “return the license to the judge of the probate court ... within 30 days after the date of the marriage” (§ 19-3-30(c)).
sources: new words: the framing of the two days
courthouse-same.alt: A creek running over rock through a forest of fall leaves

courthouse-day.heading: A threshold,
courthouse-day.text:
The hundred-foot rope bridge isn't a gimmick. It's a threshold. The moment you step onto it, you leave the ground behind. By the time you reach the other side, something in your chest has shifted.

Most elopement couples bring their closest people. The bridge is rated for eight people at one time, everyone counted: on the bridge that is the two of you, your officiant, and up to five more, your photographer among them.

Not included: hair and makeup, though we are glad to point you toward artists we trust; your marriage license; and food and drink beyond the champagne toast.
sources: new words: "Most elopement couples bring their closest people."

courthouse-season.heading: Any season,
courthouse-season.text:
Wildflower brings soft light and mountain laurel. Canopy Green brings fireflies. Color Turn is a cathedral of gold and crimson. Frost Season strips the canopy to its bones and reveals views you can't see the rest of the year.

Rain in the mountains is its own kind of magic, and your photographer will love it. Every couple receives a weather contingency plan. The canopy provides natural protection.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/elopements.py:61 ("We have seven seasons" left out: the line names four)
loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/elopements.py:63 (its "We've hosted ceremonies" left out: no ceremony is hosted yet)

proposal.heading: Somewhere they will remember
proposal.text:
If you're going to ask, ask somewhere they'll remember the walk to.

Around the last curve the laurel opens, and there's the bridge: a hundred feet of it, sixty feet up, strung with small warm lights. Halfway across, you stop noticing the height and start noticing the silence. You could ask there. Or on the deck, or by the fire.

Tell us when you write, and the treehouse will be ready before you walk them in: things like champagne and rose petals, set out ahead of you.

You bring the ring. The lights come on by themselves.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:143-148 (the Writer's proposal block: new words; "Ten minutes under the trees" left out; the "We'll keep it quiet" question left out)
loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/experiences.py:47 (Romance Package: an add-on still Mick's open question)

proposals-where.heading: On the bridge, by the fire,
proposals-where.text:
The Rope Bridge. A hundred feet of suspended bridge between two white oaks, sixty feet up and strung with small warm lights. Stop halfway across and turn around.

The Fire Circle. A boulder fire pit set at the four compass points, ringed with ferns. Sit close to the fire after dark and ask with the whole forest listening.

The Canopy Deck. The private deck of your treehouse, sixty feet in the air. Nothing above you but sky, nothing around you but the canopy.
sources: loxleyforest@8feb5c7:scripts/site/pages/proposals.py:26-36 (SPOTS; "the Compass Fire Pit" is the Fire Circle by canon/voice.md law 7)
proposals-where.alt: The rope bridge at night, its rails strung with warm lights

proposals-how.heading: Leave the setting to us.
proposals-how.text:
Tell us the date you have in mind and how you want it to feel. Golden hour on the bridge or a fire after dark. Quiet, or with a photographer there to catch it.

Things like flowers and champagne on ice, ready where you plan to ask.

The rest of the night is yours, in the treehouse at the far end of the bridge. The treehouse is yours until morning: a queen bed framed by panoramic windows, a private deck above the forest floor, and the forest all around you.
sources: loxleyforest@8feb5c7:scripts/site/pages/proposals.py:40-48 (STEPS; "lanterns" left out: the agreement bars open flame and sky lanterns)
loxleyforest@8feb5c7:scripts/site/pages/proposals.py:145 (after the yes; its late checkout left out: canon/voice.md law 7)

propose-sunrise.heading: Preacher's Rock
propose-sunrise.text:
A short climb with a massive reward: one of the best views in North Georgia, on the Appalachian Trail. It faces southeast, so at sunrise you're above the clouds.

Leave the treehouse by 6:30 AM. The best effort-to-reward ratio in the area.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/local_guide.py:42-45 ("2 miles round trip" left out: a distance in miles with no fact row)
propose-sunrise.alt: A leaf-covered trail through rhododendron and tall hardwoods

propose-sunset.heading: Kaya Vineyard
propose-sunset.text: 270-degree mountain views from a hilltop, the most dramatic vista of any winery in the area. Get there an hour before sunset with a glass in hand. The best free sunset show in North Georgia.

propose-water.heading: A lake loop,
propose-water.text:
Lake Zwerner is an easy, scenic loop around the reservoir. Flat, beautiful, accessible. Coffee at Jethro's first, then the loop. The perfect easy morning.

Amicalola Falls is the waterfall to see. The East Ridge Loop gives you the best of it. Stop at B.J. Reece Orchards on the way back for cider and doughnuts.

Raven Cliff Falls is for guests who actually want to hike: a stunning waterfall, stream crossings, beautiful forest, real hiking.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/local_guide.py:38-41 ("the tallest cascading waterfall in Georgia" left to the fact row, which cites the park)
propose-water.alt: A waterfall spilling over mossy rock in a green summer forest

propose-here.eyebrow: And one you can stay at
propose-here.heading: Ask the question
propose-here.text:
Halfway across the bridge, you stop noticing the height and start noticing the silence. That is a good place to ask.

Ask on the bridge at golden hour, by the fire after dark, or on the deck with nothing around you but trees. Tell us which, and we'll help you get the moment right.

Then stay the night. Wake up engaged in the trees.
propose-here.alt: The rope bridge deck leading through the canopy to the treehouse at dusk

romantic-stay.heading: Sixty feet changes
romantic-stay.text:
You'll fall asleep sixty feet in the air with nothing above you but stars and nothing below you but the creek rolling through the forest floor.

At ground level, a forest is beautiful. At sixty feet, it's transcendent. You're level with the hawks. Sound works differently up here: the wind moves through the leaves like a living thing, and the silence between gusts is the deepest quiet you've heard in years.

The canopy at sunrise isn't a view. It's a slow-motion event.

romantic-seasons.heading: Fall color.
romantic-seasons.text:
In spring, wildflowers blanket the forest floor and mountain laurel blooms along every trail. The waterfalls run full, and the forest smells like rain and new growth.

In summer, fireflies light the forest at dusk: in June and July the canopy lights up from the inside. Long evenings on the deck. The canopy is so thick the only light is green.

In fall, color at elevation arrives earlier and lasts longer. The canopy turns gold, then crimson, then amber. The most dramatic season, and the most popular. Book early.

In winter, the bare canopy shows views the leaves keep secret, and the fire pit feels essential.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/local_guide.py:101-112 (the seasons; the Butterfly Farm's date and the tubing's cost left out)
romantic-seasons.alt: From above in fall: the treehouse canvas showing through a canopy of orange, red and gold

romantic-evening.heading: Stars and s'mores,
romantic-evening.text: Graham crackers, chocolate, marshmallows, and a fire you built yourself. The stars do the rest.
romantic-evening.alt: The stone fire pit on the forest floor, ringed with ferns

anniversary.heading: Give one night of them
anniversary.text:
You've had years together. Give one night of them to the trees.

Walk in under the canopy. Cross a hundred feet of bridge with the lights coming on. Eat by the fire. Sleep sixty feet up in the oaks.

Before you go, sit down at the desk. There's stationery there, a pen and an envelope. Write to each other, or to who you want to be a year from now. Seal it and leave it with us. In twelve months it arrives at your door, and you read what you wrote a year ago.

That's the anniversary. The next one starts with a letter.
sources: loxley-rescue/docs/briefs/2026-10-29-writer-pseo-copy.md:136-141 (the Writer's anniversary block: new words; The Letter is still Mick's open question)

anniversary-home.heading: A home
anniversary-home.text:
This is not a cabin with a view. This is a home in the sky, suspended in a canopy of white oak and beech that has stood for over a century.

A queen bed framed by panoramic windows that turn every morning into a painting you've never seen before. A private deck suspended above the forest floor. A pizza oven on your sky deck, because even pizza is better in the canopy.

What we don't include: televisions. You won't need one.
anniversary-home.alt: The bed beneath the treehouse windows in warm light

anniversary-evening.heading: Your stay is a story,
anniversary-evening.text:
Unpack. Step onto the deck. Realize you're sixty feet in the air and there isn't a single sound except wind through leaves.

Fire up the pizza oven on the sky deck. Open the bottle you brought. Burn the first pizza. Laugh about it. Nail the second one.

Build a fire. Roast marshmallows. Look up.

Fall asleep to absolute silence, sixty feet above the forest floor.
sources: loxleyforest/scripts/site/pages/book.py:51 (its Milky Way line left out: the site puts the clearest stars November to early spring)
anniversary-evening.alt: The pizza oven on the sky deck

honeymoon.heading: This part is
honeymoon.text:
The wedding was for everyone. This part is for the two of you.

A hundred feet of bridge, and a canvas treehouse sixty feet up in the oaks. No television. The Wi-Fi is a hotspot you have to switch on, and you don't have to.

One night, ask for After Dark: champagne, strawberries, a blanket on the deck, and the sky you've never actually seen. From November through early spring, with the leaves down, that sky is all of it. In summer the stars come in pockets between the branches, and the fire table keeps you out there longer.

In the morning, nowhere to be.

honeymoon-room.heading: Intimate
honeymoon-room.text:
A queen bed framed by panoramic windows, and a chandelier over it on a dimmer. The details you'll find during your stay are Livy's hand: the warmth of the light, every window placed to frame the canopy, a room that feels intimate instead of exposed.

It was Livy who insisted on a full bathroom in the canopy, a waterfall shower sixty feet above the forest floor.
honeymoon-room.alt: Inside the treehouse: a bed, a long wooden bench and tall windows onto the forest

honeymoon-gift.heading: Or the gift
honeymoon-gift.text: The Golden Arrow is a gift of three nights in the treehouse at Loxley Forest, and the Dawn Table. Champagne brunch across the bridge. Pizza night in the trees.
